cells.tense: Something you kept working on is giving off light on its own this season.
cells.ask: Put one finished thing in front of one person this week and let it stand without adding anything to it.
cells.core:
You spent a long time building something, and now it carries its own light. The shine isn't coming from effort you're spending today; it's coming from the thing being done enough. That's a different feeling than pushing — quieter, and it holds even when you step back.

The pull you're following is still there, and it's yours, not borrowed. What's arriving now is the next piece in this, and you're allowed to meet it the same way you met the last one. Let one finished piece be seen by one person this week, unpolished and unadded-to. That costs you the safety of keeping it closed, and it keeps the light honest.
cells.sheetLine: The light comes from what you finished, not from what you're pushing.

cells.tense: You're selling a bright future hard enough that the present can't get a word in.
cells.ask: Set a timer for ten minutes, describe what's in the room in plain words, and stop there for the night.
cells.core:
You keep describing a good outcome before it's here, and you're arguing for it with more force than the facts carry. It sounds hopeful. Underneath, you're bracing — staying ahead of a future you can't control. The brightness you're casting lands on the next room, and the room you're actually in stays dim.

What's arriving is smaller and more ordinary than the version you're pitching. You can meet it by tolerating not knowing what happens — that's a skill, not a mood. Take ten minutes and describe what's physically around you, one thing at a time, without turning it into the next step. Do that and the shine goes back to coming from what's actually grown.

cells.tense: You kept faith with something that never bloomed, and you're still standing where it didn't.
cells.ask: Give ten slow minutes to one living thing you're part of — a person, a skill, a plant — and don't grade it afterward.
cells.core:
There's a flatness in you that rest won't touch. Things you cared for didn't come up, and you learned not to expect much. So when something new arrives — an idea, an opening, a reason to care — you let it pass without picking it up. Nothing has gone wrong with the desire itself. It's just running low.

What helps isn't manufacturing a brighter feeling. It's feeding one small growing thing you're already connected to, gently, without grading it — care that doesn't have to exhaust you to count. Hold it loosely, without gripping, and let it develop at its own pace. The ask is ten minutes of that. Nothing more to prove, and nothing to fix tonight.

cells.tense: Something of yours is already glowing, or it's gone quiet, and you're not saying which.
cells.ask: In a normal sentence, out loud, say you made one good thing — no qualifiers, no laughing it off.
cells.core:
Something you built reached its own point and it's giving off light — or it stopped months ago and nobody has heard you say so. Either way you're not claiming it. You talk about it like it happened around you rather than through you, as if the shine belonged to the thing and not to anyone who made it.

The move here is smaller and older than you'd guess: just carry the fact that the thing is good, without forcing it to be more. That's not a trick, it's holding what's already true. Say out loud, once, in an ordinary sentence, that you made something good — no qualifier tacked on, no joke to soften it. The light doesn't need the credit. You do.

attempts.check: The record doesn't say the person's past, motives, or what happened; the Too Little cell must not say what caused the exhaustion. A reader could object that 'radiance' is too grand for what they feel, so I keep it as an observable thing—what shows in a face or a carried tone. The asks stay useful even if my read is wrong: this seat is about what's entering, and each ask is one act of noticing or meeting what's already arriving. I'll cut the sentence that would have praised their growth—it serves the house's wish more than the person.

A reader could fairly object that they aren't exhausted at all, just unbothered — closer to the Unacknowledged face — so each ask has to stand as one visible act even if my read of the status is off. The sentence I cut was the one that explained the map back to them; it served my wish to be understood more than it served them. All four asks are doable today, with no money, no safe person required, and no promised result.
